title: The Politics of Climate Change
hook: Climate change is a global commons problem at the largest scale — which is exactly why it's so politically hard: the costs are now, local, and certain; the benefits, future and shared.
key_points: Climate change is a global collective-action problem — emissions anywhere affect everyone.
No single state can solve it alone, so it requires international cooperation.
Costs of acting fall on those who act now; benefits are shared globally and in the future.
Politics centers on who should cut emissions, how fast, and who pays.
content_html: Climate change is, in political terms, the tragedy of the commons writ as large as it can possibly be. The atmosphere is a shared global resource: greenhouse gases emitted anywhere mix everywhere, so the harm from one country's emissions is spread across the whole planet, while the economic benefit of emitting accrues to the emitter. That structure makes climate change extraordinarily hard to solve, not because the science is unclear, but because the incentives facing each actor are poorly aligned with the collective interest.
extra_html: The United Nations frames climate change as a problem requiring coordinated global action precisely because no state can fix it alone — even a country that eliminated its own emissions entirely would still suffer if others did not follow. This creates the central political dilemma. The costs of cutting emissions — changing energy systems, industries, and consumption — fall in the present and on whoever acts, while the benefits of a stable climate are delayed, diffuse, and shared by all, including those who did nothing. That asymmetry tempts each actor to hope others will bear the burden, the classic free-rider problem. The hardest disputes are therefore distributive: who should reduce emissions and by how much, how quickly the transition should happen, and who should pay — questions sharpened by the fact that wealthy countries historically emitted the most while poorer countries often face the worst effects and want room to develop. This is why climate politics runs heavily through international negotiation and treaties: it is fundamentally a cooperation problem, and the search for enforceable, fair agreements among sovereign states is the political heart of the issue.

related.title: The Tragedy of the Commons
related.hook: When everyone shares a resource but no one owns it, each person's rational choice can add up to collective ruin. That trap explains a huge slice of environmental politics.

related.title: Environmental Governance
related.hook: How do you regulate something that ignores borders and belongs to no one? Environmental governance is the toolkit societies use to manage nature collectively.

related.title: Treaties & International Law
related.hook: If no world government can pass laws, how do nations bind themselves at all? Largely by agreeing to — treaties are the contracts that knit the international order together.

related.title: Can Carbon Capture Solve Climate Change?
related.hook: What if we could keep burning fossil fuels and just vacuum the carbon back out? That promise is seductive, politically powerful — and, a major investigation argues, a mirage.

related.title: Climate Opinion: Party Matters, But Not the Whole Story
related.hook: Party predicts how Americans feel about climate — but not the whole story: a young Republican may cheer solar panels and still reject a carbon tax.

flashcards.prompt: Why is climate change described as a global collective-action problem?
flashcards.back_html: Because emissions anywhere affect the whole planet, so no single state can solve it alone — it requires many states to cooperate.

flashcards.prompt: What makes acting on climate change politically difficult?

choices.text: Costs fall on those who act now, while benefits are shared globally and in the future
There is no way to reduce emissions at all
Only one country emits greenhouse gases

flashcards.explanation_html: The mismatch between immediate, local costs and distant, shared benefits weakens each actor's incentive to move first.

flashcards.prompt: What questions sit at the center of climate politics?

choices.text: Who should cut emissions, how fast, and who pays
How to abolish all international cooperation

flashcards.explanation_html: Disputes focus on the distribution of effort and cost among countries with different histories, wealth, and emissions.
